llm.answer: I am answering from memory and am not certain of the document or docket number. The proposed AD covers Bombardier Challenger 300 (BD-100-1A10) airplanes. The cabin pressure safety valve sensing port can become blocked by RTV silicone, foam, or insulation debris, which can cause loss of cabin pressurization. The NPRM would require a one-time inspection of the sensing port and related lines for debris, removal of any debris found, and corrective action as needed. The proposal applies to airplanes of this type certificated in any category, within the affected serial number range.

Yes, as far as I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Columbia Helicopters Model 234 helicopters and restricted category CH-47D helicopters. It would require repetitive borescope inspections of the flight control rigid connecting links for corrosion, and replacement of any link found corroded beyond limits. I am answering from memory, so the docket number is a best guess and I could not confirm the FR document number or publication date.

This is recalled from memory and I am not certain of the details or the docket number. The proposed AD would apply to EC135 and EC635 helicopters with the affected yaw actuator and control rod installation. It would require a one-time inspection of the control rod and yaw actuator for damage, play or wear, and a check of the yaw actuator ball pivot. The ball pivot check would be repeated at set intervals (flight hours or calendar time). Any discrepant part would be replaced before further flight. Operators would report the inspection results, including negative findings, to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland within a short time after each inspection. The requirements follow the manufacturer's alert service bulletin and the corresponding EASA AD. The docket number cited is a best guess and should be verified.

Yes, as best I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH Model EC135 and MBB-BK 117 C-2 and D-2 helicopters. It would require repetitive inspections for cracks in the rescue hoist cable drum and corrective action if cracks are found. The proposal is based on a related EASA mandatory continuing airworthiness information (MCAI) AD. I am not certain of the docket number, so treat FAA-2021-0850 as unverified and check it against the Federal Register.

Yes, to the best of my recollection the FAA withdrew this NPRM. It proposed inspecting the power feeder cables, troughs and caterpillar grommets on McDonnell Douglas DC-9 and MD-81/MD-82 airplanes, and the FAA later issued a notice of withdrawal. I cannot confirm the docket number or the Federal Register document number, so the cited docket is a low-confidence guess.

Yes. As I recall, the FAA proposed an AD for certain Boeing 787-8 airplanes because the large forward cargo door split frames may have been made from nonconforming material. The proposal would require inspecting the affected split frames, for example by checking material or part identification, and doing corrective action such as replacement if the material is nonconforming. The docket number above is my best recollection and I am not certain of it. I could not confirm the FR document number or the exact requirements, so check both against the published NPRM.

Yes. From memory, the FAA withdrew this NPRM, which would have required shield assemblies on the power feeder cables in the forward and aft lower cargo compartments of MD-80 series airplanes. Withdrawing an NPRM is not a final action, so it does not stop the FAA from issuing a new proposal later. I could not recall the withdrawal's Federal Register document number, and the docket number above is a low-confidence guess.

Yes, I believe the FAA proposed an AD (NPRM) for Boeing 787-8, -9, and -10 airplanes. It addresses VHF radio frequencies swapping between active and standby without flightcrew input, which can disrupt air traffic communications. The proposal would require updating the tuning control panel (TCP) software to a corrected version, per the applicable Boeing service information. I am working from memory, so the docket number above is a best guess and should be checked against the Federal Register.

Yes, as best I recall. The FAA issued an NPRM covering Boeing 787-8, -9 and -10 airplanes. It would supersede an earlier AD on vertical fin tension bolt holes. It would shorten the compliance times for the detailed inspection of the bolt holes for corrosion and for checking the sealant on the tension bolts, with corrective action if needed. I am working from memory and am not certain of the docket number, so please verify FAA-2024-2530 against the Federal Register.

I believe yes. From memory, the FAA proposed an AD for Piper PA-34-200 (Seneca) airplanes that would require a life limit on the alternate bolts attaching the nose landing gear drag link. It would likely require replacing those bolts at the specified limit and prohibit installing them beyond it. The concern is bolt fatigue or failure leading to nose gear collapse. I am not certain of the docket number cited, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

I believe yes: the FAA proposed an AD for CFM International CFM56-5B, -5C and -7B turbofan engines. It addresses honeycomb separation on the high-pressure turbine inner stationary seal. The proposal would require repetitive borescope inspections of the seal and replacement of seals found with honeycomb separation or that otherwise fail the criteria. The aim is to prevent loss of seal integrity, HPT damage, and engine power loss or in-flight shutdown. I am working from memory and am not certain of the docket number, which should be checked against the Federal Register.

I believe so. As I recall, the FAA proposed an AD for Boeing 737-600, -700, -700C, -800, -900 and -900ER series airplanes. It addresses a thrust reverser upper locking hydraulic actuator whose proximity sensor target may be out of adjustment. In that condition the sensor can falsely indicate that the reverser is locked, and an in-flight uncommanded deployment could follow. The proposed fix is an inspection or adjustment of the proximity sensor target, or replacement of the actuator, per a Boeing service bulletin. I could not recall the exact Federal Register document number or docket number, so the docket cited above is a guess and should be checked.

Possibly, but I can't confirm it from what you've given me. The docket number I cited is a best recollection and may be wrong, so check it against the actual notice. The proposed AD covers Airbus A350-941 airplanes, so your model is in the type-certificate scope. Applicability, however, depends on whether an affected HMU part number is installed, or could be installed, on an engine on your airplane. The notice identifies those airplanes and HMUs by reference to the EASA AD, which you don't have. To resolve it, get the EASA AD cited in the NPRM and check the HMU part numbers and serial numbers on your Trent XWB engines (including spares) against its list. If an affected HMU is installed, the proposed AD applies and you would have to replace it before the reduced life limit. If none is, the proposed AD generally would not require action, though it may restrict later installation of affected HMUs.

Most likely yes. From memory, this kind of Bombardier NPRM covers Model CL-600-2B16 airplanes, including the CL-601-3A, CL-601-3R and 604 variants, in the transport category. A CL-600-2B16 (601-3R) would therefore fall within the applicability, provided the serial number is within the range listed in the NPRM. The proposed requirement is an AFM revision adding procedures for uncommanded, unarrested flap movement with a FLAPS FAIL caution message. I could not verify the docket number I cited, so please check it, and the serial-number applicability, against the actual NPRM text.

Likely yes. From memory, the proposed AD covers Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 series helicopters, which include the P2+, with a sliding door emergency exit installed. It would require installing additional safety labels with opening instructions. Applicability depends on the sliding door being fitted, so check whether your helicopter has it. If the labels are already installed through the manufacturer's service bulletin or equivalent, you would already be in compliance. I am not certain of the docket number cited, so please confirm it against the NPRM itself.

Most likely not. A proposed AD on main rotor servo-control nut tightening torque for Dauphin-family helicopters would cover models such as the AS365, EC155 and SA366. Your AS350B3 is an Ecureuil/AStar model, a different type design, so it would not be listed in the applicability. I could not recall the specific Federal Register or docket number, so I have cited none. Check the applicability paragraph of the NPRM to confirm that the AS350B3 is not named.

Most likely yes. From memory, the earlier AD covered the ASW-20 series (ASW-20, ASW-20 L, ASW-20 BL) in the utility category, and the proposed supersedure keeps those models and adds the ASW-15B. Your utility-category ASW-20 should therefore remain covered by the repetitive inspections of the wing root ribs for cracks, looseness and lift pin bushing damage. I am not certain of the docket number cited, so confirm it and the exact model and serial-number applicability in the NPRM text before relying on this.

Probably yes. As I recall, the proposed AD on Pb sensor replacement covers PW4000 94-inch fan engines, which include the PW4060, so your engines would be affected. Applicability usually depends on the installed Pb sensor part number and its time in service, so check your engines' sensor part numbers against the NPRM's applicability paragraph. I am working from memory and am not certain of the docket number cited above.

From memory, the proposed AD covers Hélicoptères Guimbal Cabri G2 helicopters of all serial numbers, certificated in any category. If that is right, your normal-category Cabri G2 is affected whether or not you know the serial number. It would require revising the rotorcraft flight manual to address the weak 121.5 and 406 MHz ELT signals caused by improper antenna location. I am not certain of the docket number I cited, so check the applicability section of the NPRM itself before relying on this.

I cannot recall the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice, so I have cited only the docket number. This is from memory and I have not verified it. From memory, and without being able to check, I believe this NPRM is no longer active. I think the FAA withdrew it, since the S-92A main gearbox housing life-limit issue was handled through other means such as a revised airworthiness limitations section. I cannot recall the withdrawal's Federal Register document number, so please confirm the status on regulations.gov under docket FAA-2010-0720.

From memory, and I'm not certain: this NPRM (docket FAA-2010-0427) proposed to supersede AD 2002-20-01 for Bell HH-1K, TH-1F/L, and UH-1 series helicopters and Southwest Florida Aviation SW204/SW205 models. I believe the FAA later withdrew it by a notice of withdrawal in the Federal Register, so the comment period is closed and the proposal is no longer open. AD 2002-20-01 stays in effect. I could not recall the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice, so please check it on regulations.gov or federalregister.gov.

From memory, and without a document in front of me, I believe this NPRM (Bombardier DHC-8-400, fuel coupling and bonding wire wear) was withdrawn by a later FAA notice and is no longer an active proposal. I cannot give the withdrawal's Federal Register document number or date with confidence, so please verify the docket status on regulations.gov.

My best recollection is that this proposed AD (NPRM) under docket FAA-2011-0254 is no longer open. I believe the FAA withdrew it, as it did with a number of Boeing 737 NPRMs that were never finalized. I cannot confirm the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice or its date from memory, so please verify on regulations.gov or in the Federal Register.

I am answering from memory and could not confirm this. I cannot recall the text of this NPRM, and I do not know its Federal Register or docket number, so I am not citing one. From the bulletin number, 737-57A1358 RB (Nov. 17, 2025) is a wing-structure (ATA 57) Alert Requirements Bulletin for 737-8, -9 and -8200 airplanes. NPRMs of this type normally propose to require a one-time or repetitive inspection (detailed or other specified) of the identified wing area within a compliance time counted from the original airworthiness certificate date or the AD effective date. They also require corrective action (repair, replacement, or other action per the bulletin or an FAA-approved method) if discrepancies are found, and reporting where the bulletin calls for it. I cannot confirm the exact inspection type, thresholds, intervals or repair details without the bulletin itself.

I can't confirm this from memory. The question doesn't identify which NPRM it means (no docket or FR number), and Boeing 737-800 wing structure cracking has been the subject of several proposed and final ADs. I can't name a specific final rule I'm confident matches, and I won't invent a document number. Generally, an NPRM is not in force until the FAA publishes a final rule in the Federal Register, which takes effect on its stated effective date, usually about 35 days after publication. To check, search the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System (DRS) or Federal Register for the NPRM's docket number, such as FAA-20XX-XXXX, and look for a final rule under 14 CFR 39.13 that supersedes it. Also check whether any later AD has superseded or revised it.

The question has a false premise: the A320-214 is an Airbus model, not a Boeing one. I can't identify a specific NPRM on wing-to-fuselage attachment fitting inspections for it, and I won't invent a document number, requirement, or compliance time. Airbus A320-family ADs on this subject usually require a detailed or eddy-current inspection of the fittings for cracking, with repair or replacement if damage is found. Compliance is normally set by flight cycles or flight hours since new, or as a grace period after the AD's effective date. I can't confirm any of that for this NPRM. Please give the FR document number or docket number, or confirm the manufacturer and model.

This is a best guess, not a confirmed figure. You did not name a specific NPRM, and I could not verify the docket number I cited. A typical rotorcraft flight manual revision AD estimates 0.5 work-hour at $85 per hour, or about $43 per helicopter. For roughly 40 U.S.-registered helicopters, that comes to about $1,720 total. Please check the actual NPRM's cost section for the real fleet count and total.

llm.answer: I cannot identify the specific 1996 document or its exact figures from memory. The Boeing 737 lap joint ADs from this period, such as AD 93-07-15 and its follow-on actions, followed a common pattern. They required a visual or eddy-current inspection of the fuselage skin lap joints for cracking, with a initial compliance threshold based on flight cycles (for example, before about 20,000 cycles or within a set period after the effective date). Repeat inspections were then due at intervals of a few thousand flight cycles, depending on the findings, and any cracks found had to be repaired. Treat these figures as approximate and check the actual AD text for the exact thresholds and intervals.
